title: Matching specialised cells to their jobs
examples: How is a red blood cell adapted?
Why are nerve cells so long?

figure.name: x-sort
figure.question: What job is each cell built for?

explain.say: Think of a football team: a goalkeeper, defenders, strikers, each built for a job. Your body works the same way. Its cells are specialised, which means shaped for one special job. Let's sort some!

draw.text: Matching specialised cells to their jobs

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: What job is each cell built for?

explain.say: Look at the first group, carry things. A red blood cell has no nucleus and a dented shape, so it holds lots of oxygen. Xylem cells join into hollow pipes for water. Which one do you think carries water in a plant?

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: What job is each cell built for?

explain.say: Now the move things group. A muscle cell is packed with mitochondria for energy, and a sperm cell has a tail to swim. Ciliated cells have tiny hairs that sweep mucus out of your airways. Which one swims?

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: What job is each cell built for?

explain.say: See the send signals group? A nerve cell can be very long, up to a metre in your leg, so it carries messages quickly. Light-sensing cells in your eye catch light. Why might a long cell send a message faster?

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: What job is each cell built for?

explain.say: Last group: soak things up. Root hair cells and gut lining cells both have a huge surface area. Excellent sorting! Challenge: next time you breathe, picture the ciliated cells sweeping dust out of your lungs.

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: What job is each cell built for?

faq.a: A specialised cell has a special shape and special parts that suit one job, like carrying oxygen, sending signals or swimming. Cells become specialised as an organism develops, which is called differentiation.

faq.q: How is a red blood cell adapted?
faq.a: It has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen. Its biconcave shape, pushed in on both sides, gives a large surface area, and it is small and bendy enough to squeeze through capillaries.
asks: Tell me about the red blood cell

faq.q: Why are nerve cells so long?
faq.a: A long nerve cell can carry an electrical message from your spinal cord all the way to your toes without a gap. Some nerve cells in your legs are about a metre long.
asks: Tell me about the nerve cell

faq.q: How is a sperm cell adapted?
faq.a: A sperm cell has a tail to swim, many mitochondria to release energy for swimming, and a head holding half the father's DNA, with enzymes to get into the egg.
asks: Tell me about the sperm cell

faq.a: Ciliated cells line your airways. Their tiny hairs, called cilia, beat together to sweep mucus with trapped dust and germs up to your throat.

facts: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.
Some human nerve cells, running from the spine to the toes, are about one metre long.

quiz.say: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
quiz.show: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?

options.show: To make room for more haemoglobin
options.say: To make room for more haemoglobin

quiz.why: Without a nucleus there is more space for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen.

wrong.1: Without a nucleus, red blood cells cannot divide at all.
wrong.2: Red blood cells are carried along by the blood; they do not swim.

quiz.say: Which cell is adapted to sweep mucus out of the airways?
quiz.show: Which cell is adapted to sweep mucus out of the airways?
quiz.why: Ciliated cells have tiny beating hairs that move mucus up and out of the airways.

wrong.0: Root hair cells are in plant roots and absorb water.
wrong.2: Muscle cells contract to move body parts, not mucus.
